title: Occlusion-aware Projection Graphic
author: strawberry-ramune
selftext:
It's used for drawing textures which bend along 3D meshes. 

AI Description:   
  
A reusable ProjectionGraphic with texture/material, transform, box/frustum shape, fade distances, blend mode, receiver mask, normal limit, priority, and lifetime.

After opaque geometry writes the scene depth buffer, the engine reconstructs visible world positions and applies projections in screen space. This lets one graphic conform to terrain, rocks, stairs, and static world geometry without re-rendering those meshes.

Features:

Receiver classification buffer — terrain, buildings, characters, foliage, water, UI-world objects, and so on write a compact decal/receiver category during the main render. Each projection has an allow-mask, so a ground rune can affect terrain and stone floors but never players, trees, or sky.

Normal and depth filters — reject surfaces that are too steep, too far above/below the projector, or facing the wrong direction. This prevents terrain circles from smearing up walls, appearing on bridge undersides, or bleeding through geometry.

GPU-driven culling and tile lists — frustum- and distance-cull projections first, then bin survivors into screen tiles or clusters on the GPU. Each pixel evaluates only the small list of projections overlapping its tile—not every decal active in the map.

Instancing, batching, and texture atlases — hundreds of identical footprints, spell circles, impact marks, and environmental effects share one material and a few draws. Texture arrays/atlases prevent constant GPU state changes and texture swapping.

Projection budget and LOD system — give high-importance nearby projections full quality; fade, simplify, lower resolution, or drop distant/obscured low-priority ones. Useful for when you will have many players using abilities in one place. 

Terrain-conforming mesh fallback — reserve generated conforming meshes for exceptional huge seals, boss arenas, and cinematic effects. Normal projections handle everyday gameplay cheaply; meshes handle the rare cases where art direction needs perfect long-distance clarity.

Gameplay-to-visual separation — the network layer replicates a compact effect event: effect ID, seed, origin, direction, start time, and owner. Each client creates the local projection from that data. The server never needs to synchronize pixels or decal meshes.

Lifetime, pooling, and deterministic cleanup — projection instances come from pools, expire or fade on a budgeted schedule, and can be recreated from effect events. No per-cast allocation churn, which keeps hectic combat smooth.

Editor and command-bus support — place, resize, rotate, mask, and preview projections in the world editor; inspect their GPU cost and active tile coverage. That makes the system usable by both humans and AI-assisted content workflow.
